transcript.heading: News Report One (American Female)
paras: A new study has found that mindfulness meditation can significantly reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression, and may be as effective as some antidepressant medications for mild to moderate cases, according to researchers at Harvard Medical School. The study followed over 400 adults with anxiety and depression who participated in an 8-week mindfulness-based stress reduction program. The program included weekly meditation classes, daily home practice, and instruction in mindfulness techniques like breathing exercises and body scans. The researchers found that participants showed significant reductions in anxiety and depression symptoms, and these improvements lasted for at least six months after the program ended. Researchers say that mindfulness meditation works by changing how the brain responds to stress and negative emotions, and it can be a valuable tool for improving mental health. They note that meditation is not a replacement for professional mental health care, but it can be a helpful addition to treatment.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: The city of London has announced plans to build over 100 kilometers of new "quiet ways" bicycle routes across the city, as part of its efforts to encourage more people to cycle and reduce traffic and air pollution. Unlike traditional bike lanes that run along busy roads, quiet ways are cycle routes that use quieter side streets, parks, and paths away from heavy traffic. The goal is to make cycling feel safer and more comfortable for people who don't currently cycle because they're intimidated by busy roads. The city says that increasing cycling will reduce traffic congestion, improve air quality, reduce carbon emissions, and improve public health by encouraging more physical activity. The quiet ways program is part of London's broader plan to become a more bike-friendly city and to reduce its dependence on cars. The city also plans to improve cycling infrastructure at major intersections and add more bike parking throughout the city.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Researchers have developed a new artificial intelligence system that can diagnose eye diseases as accurately as expert doctors, according to a study published in the journal Nature Medicine. The AI system was trained on thousands of retinal scans to detect conditions like diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and macular degeneration—diseases that can cause blindness if not caught early. In tests, the AI system was able to diagnose these conditions with about the same accuracy as experienced ophthalmologists. Researchers say that this technology could be especially useful in areas where there aren't enough eye doctors, allowing more people to get screened and treated before they lose their vision. The AI system could also help speed up diagnosis and reduce wait times for patients in areas that do have doctors. The technology is still being tested and refined, but researchers hope it could be widely available within the next few years.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Emily): Hey Jack, I heard you just got back from your trip to Scotland. How was it?
Man (Jack): It was amazing! Scotland is so beautiful—mountains, lakes, castles... I had the best time. I can't believe I waited so long to go.
Woman: I'm so jealous! I've always wanted to go to Scotland. What did you do there?

Man: Well, I spent a few days in Edinburgh first. That's such a cool city—so much history, and the castle is incredible. I walked around the Old Town, visited the castle, went to some museums... I could have spent a whole week just in Edinburgh.
Woman: That sounds great. Did you go to the Highlands too?

Man: Yeah! I rented a car and drove up to the Highlands for a few days. Oh my god, the scenery is absolutely stunning—mountains, lochs, waterfalls... it's like something out of a movie. I did some hiking, visited some castles, and even tried some whisky at a distillery.
Woman: That sounds amazing. What was the weather like? I've heard it rains a lot in Scotland.

Man: Oh, it definitely rained. A lot. But honestly, the rain just added to the atmosphere. The Highlands look even more dramatic when it's misty and rainy. I just made sure to bring a good rain jacket and waterproof shoes, and it was fine.
Woman: Good to know. What about the food? I've heard Scottish food is... interesting.

Man: Ha, it's actually better than I expected! I had some amazing seafood—fresh salmon, oysters, mussels. And I even tried haggis, which is that famous Scottish dish made from sheep's organs. I thought it would be gross, but it was actually pretty good! You just have to be open-minded about it.
Woman: Wow, I'm impressed that you tried haggis. Did you try any other traditional foods?
Man: Yeah, I had neeps and tatties—turnips and potatoes—with the haggis. And I had shortbread, which is delicious. And of course, lots of whisky.
Woman: Ha, of course. Would you recommend going? Any tips for someone planning a trip?

Man: Absolutely, I'd highly recommend it. My tips would be: bring layers and rain gear, because the weather changes fast. Rent a car if you want to see the Highlands—public transport is limited there. And don't try to do too much—Scotland is bigger than it looks, and you'll be driving a lot. Take your time and enjoy the scenery.
Woman: That's good advice. Maybe I'll plan a trip for next year. Thanks for all the tips!
Man: No problem! You'll love it. Let me know if you have more questions as you plan.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

9. What did Jack think of the weather?
10. What did Jack think of Scottish food?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (David): Hey Sarah, I need your advice. I'm thinking about getting a dog. What do you think?
Woman (Sarah): A dog? That's a big decision! Dogs are great, but they're also a lot of work. Why do you want a dog?

Man: Well, I've always loved dogs, and I've wanted one for years. Now I have a more stable job and a bigger apartment, so I think I'm finally ready. And I think having a dog would make me get out more and be more active.

Woman: That's true—dogs are great motivation to exercise. But before you get one, you need to think about whether you're really ready. How much time do you have? Dogs need a lot of attention—you have to walk them, feed them, play with them, take them to the vet...
Man: Yeah, I know. I work full-time, which is my main concern. I'm gone for about 8 hours a day. Is that too long to leave a dog alone?

Woman: Hmm, 8 hours is a long time, especially for a puppy. Puppies need a lot of attention and they can't hold it that long. But if you get an adult dog, they can usually handle being alone for 8 hours as long as they get plenty of exercise before and after work. You could also hire a dog walker to come in the middle of the day, or take the dog to doggy daycare a few days a week.
Man: That's a good point. Maybe an adult dog would be better for me than a puppy. What about breed? Do you think certain breeds are better for people who work full-time?

Woman: Yeah, definitely. Some breeds need more exercise and attention than others. If you're gone all day, you probably don't want a super high-energy breed like a border collie or a husky—they'd go crazy being alone all day. More independent breeds or lower-energy breeds might be better. But honestly, it depends more on the individual dog than the breed.
Man: What about size? I live in an apartment, so I probably don't want a huge dog.

Woman: Yeah, size is important for apartments. But don't assume that small dogs are always better for apartments—some small dogs are really high energy and bark a lot. And some big dogs are actually very calm and lazy indoors. It's more about the dog's energy level than its size.
Man: That's good to know. Should I get a dog from a shelter or buy one from a breeder?

Woman: I'd definitely recommend adopting from a shelter first. There are so many great dogs in shelters that need homes. And shelter dogs are often already house-trained and have some basic training. Plus, adoption is a lot cheaper than buying from a breeder.
Man: Yeah, I was thinking about adopting. I just worry that I won't know the dog's history or personality.

Woman: That's a valid concern, but shelter staff usually know the dogs pretty well and can help you find one that matches your lifestyle. They can tell you about the dog's energy level, how it is with people and other animals, and any behavioral issues. And many shelters let you foster a dog first to see if it's a good fit.
Man: That's a good idea. What about cost? How much does it cost to have a dog?

Woman: It depends, but it's not cheap. You have food, vet bills, grooming, toys, supplies... it adds up. I'd say at least a few hundred dollars a month, on average. And you have to be prepared for unexpected vet bills, which can be really expensive.
Man: Hmm, that's more than I thought. But I think I can afford it.

Woman: Well, it sounds like you're thinking it through, which is good. Having a dog is a big responsibility, but it's also really rewarding. Dogs are great companions and they make your life better in so many ways.
Man: Yeah, I think I'm ready. Thanks for all the advice, Sarah. You've given me a lot to think about.
Woman: No problem! Let me know if you decide to get one—I'd love to meet your new dog!

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: The history of the bicycle is a story of innovation and evolution that spans over 200 years. From the earliest wooden walking machines to the modern high-tech bikes we know today, bicycles have come a long way and have had a huge impact on transportation, society, and even women's rights.

The earliest bicycle-like invention was called the "draisine" or "running machine," invented by German baron Karl von Drais in 1817. It was made entirely of wood and had no pedals—you sat on it and pushed yourself along with your feet, like a modern balance bike. It was popular for a few years, but it was heavy, uncomfortable, and hard to steer.

In the 1860s, the first real bicycle with pedals was invented. These early bikes were called "velocipedes" or "boneshakers" because they were so uncomfortable to ride on cobblestone streets. They had iron wheels and wooden frames, and riding them was a bumpy, jarring experience.

The 1870s and 1880s saw the rise of the "penny-farthing" or high-wheel bicycle. These bikes had a huge front wheel and a tiny back wheel. The bigger the front wheel, the faster you could go. Penny-farthings were popular with young men who liked the speed and thrill, but they were also very dangerous—if you hit a bump or stopped too fast, you could go flying over the handlebars.

The modern bicycle as we know it today was invented in the 1880s. It was called the "safety bicycle" because it was much safer than the penny-farthing. It had two wheels of the same size, a chain drive to power the back wheel, and pneumatic (air-filled) tires for a smoother ride. The safety bicycle was a huge success, and it made cycling popular with everyone, including women.

The safety bicycle had a big impact on society. For the first time, ordinary people could travel quickly and cheaply without relying on horses or trains. Cycling became a popular sport and pastime. And for women, the bicycle was revolutionary—it gave them new freedom and independence, allowing them to travel on their own and participate in activities outside the home. The bicycle even played a role in the women's suffrage movement.

Today, bicycles are more popular than ever. There are billions of bicycles in the world, and they're used for everything from transportation to recreation to sport. And with growing concerns about climate change and health, cycling is becoming an increasingly important part of urban transportation.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: Animal communication is a fascinating field of study that explores how animals share information with each other. While animals don't have language in the same way humans do, they use a wide variety of methods to communicate—sounds, body language, smells, and even electrical signals. Understanding how animals communicate gives us insight into their intelligence, social lives, and emotions.

One of the most famous examples of animal communication is the honeybee's "waggle dance." When a honeybee finds a good source of food, it returns to the hive and performs a special dance that tells the other bees exactly where the food is. The direction of the dance tells the bees which direction to fly, and the length of the dance tells them how far away the food is. It's an incredibly sophisticated form of communication that was only fully understood in the 20th century.

Many animals use sound to communicate. Birds sing to attract mates and defend their territories. Whales and dolphins use complex vocalizations to communicate with each other over long distances underwater. Elephants use low-frequency rumbles that can travel through the ground for miles, allowing them to communicate with other elephants far away. And primates like chimpanzees and gorillas use a variety of calls, gestures, and facial expressions to communicate.

Body language is another important form of animal communication. Dogs wag their tails when they're happy, tuck their tails between their legs when they're scared, and bare their teeth when they're angry. Cats purr when they're content, arch their backs when they're scared, and rub against people to mark them with their scent. These are all ways that animals communicate their feelings and intentions without words.

Some animals use chemical communication—smells and pheromones—to send messages. Ants leave chemical trails that other ants follow to find food. Many mammals use scent marking to establish territory and attract mates. And even insects like moths can detect pheromones from miles away.

But while animal communication is complex and sophisticated, it's not the same as human language. Human language is symbolic—we use words that represent things, and we can combine words in infinite ways to create new meanings. Animal communication is usually more limited to specific contexts—danger, food, mating, territory. Animals don't seem to have the same kind of grammar and syntax that human language has.

Still, studying animal communication teaches us a lot about animals and about ourselves. It shows us that we're not the only creatures that can communicate, think, and feel. And it reminds us that we share this planet with many other intelligent, social beings.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: Climate change is one of the biggest challenges facing humanity today. The Earth's climate is changing faster than at any time in recorded history, and scientists overwhelmingly agree that human activities—especially the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil, and natural gas—are the main cause. Understanding climate change and what we can do about it is essential for building a sustainable future.

The greenhouse effect is a natural process that keeps the Earth warm enough for life. Gases like carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor in the atmosphere trap heat from the sun, like the glass in a greenhouse. Without the greenhouse effect, the Earth would be too cold to live on. But since the Industrial Revolution, humans have been releasing huge amounts of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere by burning fossil fuels, cutting down forests, and other activities. This is making the greenhouse effect stronger, causing the Earth to warm up.

The consequences of climate change are already being felt around the world. Global temperatures have risen by about 1 degree Celsius since pre-industrial times. Glaciers and ice sheets are melting, causing sea levels to rise. Extreme weather events like heatwaves, hurricanes, droughts, and floods are becoming more frequent and more intense. And climate change is threatening ecosystems, wildlife, and human communities around the world.

If we don't take action, the consequences could be catastrophic. Scientists warn that if global temperatures rise by more than 1.5 to 2 degrees Celsius, the changes could be irreversible and could displace hundreds of millions of people.

But it's not too late. There are many things we can do to address climate change. The most important is to transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources like solar, wind, and hydro power. We can also improve energy efficiency—using less energy to do the same things. Protecting and restoring forests and other ecosystems is also important, because trees absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

Individual actions also matter. Reducing energy use at home, driving less, eating less meat, reducing waste, and supporting sustainable businesses can all make a difference. And voting for leaders who take climate change seriously and supporting policies to reduce emissions is crucial.

Climate change is a huge challenge, but it's also an opportunity to build a better, more sustainable world. By working together, we can reduce emissions, protect the planet, and ensure a better future for generations to come.
